title: "Calculus and Optimisation"
description: "Derive gradients, Jacobians, backpropagation and optimisation rather than memorising formulas."

## The same predictor, now with learnable parameters

Suppose the prediction for each order is $\hat y_i=\beta_0+\beta_1d_i+\beta_2n_i$. We would like the parameters to minimise average squared prediction error:

$$
L(\boldsymbol\beta)=\frac1N\sum_{i=1}^{N}(\hat y_i-y_i)^2.
$$

Taking a derivative of one term tells us the sensitivity to a parameter. Collecting sensitivities gives a **gradient**:

$$
\nabla L(\boldsymbol\beta)=\frac2N X^\top(X\boldsymbol\beta-\boldsymbol y).
$$

The gradient's three entries describe how the loss changes if we independently perturb the intercept, distance coefficient or item-count coefficient.

## From derivative to an algorithm

For the simpler scalar example $L(\theta)=(\theta-3)^2$, derivative is $2(\theta-3)$. Starting at $\theta_0=0$ and taking a step of size $\eta=0.1$:

$$
\theta_1=\theta_0-0.1\,L'(\theta_0)=0-0.1(-6)=0.6.
$$

The loss decreases from 9 to 5.76. This is **one local step**, not an unconditional promise of convergence. The learning rate, curvature and function's shape all matter.

For a composition $h=g\circ f$, the chain rule computes derivatives in stages. Neural-network **backpropagation** is a systematic reverse traversal of such a computation graph.

## Learning path

Read [Vector Calculus](chapters/05-vector-calculus/index.qmd) first, including Jacobians and automatic differentiation, and then [Continuous Optimization](chapters/07-continuous-optimization/index.qmd) for gradient descent, constrained optimisation and convexity.

Try the [interactive gradient-descent experiment](interactives/gradient-descent.qmd) before moving on to the [regression loss](chapters/09-linear-regression/parameter-estimation.qmd).

~~~bash
python3 ai-mathematics/examples/delivery_ml_lab.py calculus
python3 ai-mathematics/examples/delivery_ml_lab.py optimisation
~~~

**Important distinction:** the gradient is a local mathematical property, while choosing parameters with gradient descent is an algorithm. An analytical least-squares formula is another route to the same convex quadratic optimum when its assumptions hold.
